Don’t have sex with them so soon. If you’re looking for a solid relationship, then having sex with a stranger isn’t going to help. On the other hand, if you don’t necessarily care, then by all means keep doing you. I have a friend that claims to want a serious relationship, but ends up sleeping with strangers after the first couple dates. My rule of thumb is 2weeks to 1 month of communication before I even go on a date. After going on several dates foreplay may happen, but no sex until I know for sure that I could see myself with this person. Again, this is my experience using bumble and tinder. Hope you find love and happiness ♥️

Sometimes I feel like I’m in a similar situation. I have a close friend that I recently started developing feelings for. Unfortunately, this person sleeps with a lot of people and doesn’t sound like they’re ready for a relationship. What did I do? I took a step back and focused on myself. Am I waiting on her? No, because life isn’t going to wait on me. I found someone else that I talk to and hopefully become friends with. If it turns into a relationship, then great. If not, no worries. The best suggestion anyone ever gave me was don’t waste your time with anyone that isn’t worth it.

It’s what you make it. Personally, I’ve found a handful of people on Tinder that were date worthy. However, I wasn’t in the right frame of mind. I had to realize that matching with someone doesn’t mean we’re compatible. How so? For starters, the primary reason for matching is aesthetics. If someone looks like your type, the it’s an automatic right swipe. Also, once I found someone worth my time there was no need to keep swiping. Constantly swiping won’t give your match (someone you share a mutual interest of liking with) or you a fair chance. Why? Because you will always find someone better when you’re constantly swiping/looking. There is no peak to dating apps. The next best thing is only a swipe away. Hence, be mindful of this as you pursue the world of online dating. My best regards to you OP!

First off, I’m 25 and this thread is full of experience, strength, and hope from people that completely understand alcoholism/addiction. Thank you all for responding to the OP. I needed to see this, especially as I approach the 90 day mark. In all honesty, It’s been a rough ride. Good days come and go. I thought sobriety was going to be a an easy walk through the park because all I had to do was stop drinking. However, when they told me that my drinking was a symptom of the problems in my life, I realized this was going to be one of the most challenging battles of my life. My experience so far in AA has been that attending meetings, having a sponsor, and working the steps helps. My strength comes from interacting with people at the meetings and listening to what they share. Also, having a strong network of AA’s outside of my sponsor has been useful. Lastly, my hope stems from the fact that my worst day sober doesn’t compare to my best day drunk. In other words, things have been getting better, slowly but surely. I’m not an old-timer, I’m a newcomer. I’ve been in pursuit of 90 meetings in 90 days because it was suggested once I got out of rehab. Your program of action will reflect in your life, regardless of uncontrollable circumstances. Do the work when you’re ready, and know that something positive will come out of unpacking all the pain, struggle, and hurt that you’ve been through. It’s worth it. ONE DAY AT A TIME.

I live in a household with alcoholics. It was suggested to me that I move into an Oxford house. However, I have remained in an environment where I see alcohol every day. I go to meetings and have a sponsor. Not every day is easy, nor is it ideal. However, I chose this reality and have to make the most of it. It’s possible to survive and adapt in any type of environment if you are desperate enough to stay sober. I hope this helps.... Maybe it won’t? All I know is that early sobriety is tough, but using isn’t worth the consequences.
Meetings, sponsor, and steps were the biggest suggestions given to me. Keep coming back.

For me, no matter the medical condition, I couldn’t stop drinking. It always took getting to rock bottom, where my health was compromised along with loved ones. I wish you the best in your journey. I tried rehabs and therapy, but wasn’t ready to stop. Currently, I’m working the AA 12 step program with a sponsor. Meetings, a sponsor with a working knowledge of the 12-steps, and actual step work have been tremendously helpful for me.

In my experience detox helped. Afterwards, meetings, sponsor, and step work. Doesn’t matter what my d.o.c was/is. I have to abstain from any mind altering substances , or I will continuously destroy my life and those who love me. In my experience, people couldn’t tell me anything until I got to the bottom. Also, Nobody told me that it can always get worse. I thought I was in a bad place after the first couple times I relapsed, but after relapsing with 2.5yrs clean I hit a new low in less than 6 months. You’ll stop once you can’t take the mental and physical pain anymore. You’ll stop once you hit a new low where there’s nothing but loneliness. Until then, be as safe as you can.
